Explore baseline biodiversity data curated by communities across the Salish Sea.
Galiano Island 1 Marine animals of Galiano Island (1893–2021) 20,022 records A catalogue of the marine animals reported from the waters around Galiano Island, from sponges and worms to fishes and marine mammals, bringing together historical collections and published reports with the community science observations gathered by the Biodiversity Galiano project since 2016. Records distinguish historical reports that have since been confirmed, those that remain unconfirmed, and species newly reported for the island.
Data paper: Simon et al. (2022), Biodiversity Data Journal 10: e76050
Galiano Island is located within the shared, asserted, and unceded traditional territories of the Pune’luxutth’, Quw’utsun’, Lamalchi, W̱SÁNEĆ, Hul’q’umi’num’ and SENĆOŦEN-speaking people, and on the territories of the Coast Salish people of Galiano. The island also lies within the shared, asserted, and ceded traditional territories of the Tsawwassen First Nation. These nations, along with other Hwulmuhw Mustimuhw, continue to serve as the stewards of these lands and waters, having held rights and responsibilities here since time immemorial.
Southern Gulf Islands 1 Harvey Janszen’s field journal (1973–1980) 1,296 records Plant observations from the Southern Gulf Islands, transcribed from Harvey Janszen’s field journal of 1973–1980 through the Janszen Legacy Project.
Records transcribed through the Living Data Project of the Canadian Institute of Ecology and Evolution.

The islands also lie within the shared, asserted, and ceded traditional territories of the Tsawwassen First Nation. These nations, along with other Hwulmuhw Mustimuhw, continue to serve as the stewards of these lands and waters, having held rights and responsibilities here since time immemorial.
Texada Island 2 Harvey Janszen’s field journal (1997–1999) 600 records Plant observations from Texada Island, transcribed from Harvey Janszen’s field journal of 1997–1999 through the Janszen Legacy Project.
Records transcribed through the Living Data Project of the Canadian Institute of Ecology and Evolution.
CSV Woodwardia fimbriata on Texada Island (1997) 22 records Harvey Janszen’s 1997 survey of giant chain fern (Woodwardia fimbriata) on Texada Island, assessing the status of the species there. Records note the size and condition of each population, including sites since destroyed.
GPS coordinates predate May 2000, when the US military still degraded civilian GPS signals, and may be off by up to ~100 m.
Records transcribed through the Living Data Project of the Canadian Institute of Ecology and Evolution.
CSV CSV · full journal Salish Sea 1 Diatoms of the Salish Sea (1866–2026) 11,469 records A catalogue of marine diatom occurrences across the Salish Sea, consolidating records from the published literature, morphological study of samples and molecular (DNA metabarcoding) surveys. Together, these records document the region’s diatom flora and how knowledge of it has accumulated since the first reports in 1866.
Data paper: Webber et al. (2026), Biodiversity Data Journal 14: e189060
The CSV is our curated dataset, combining our newly recorded data with records from GBIF. The GBIF dataset includes only the data generated through our research.

Our approach to detecting biodiversity change is documented in the Protocol for the Detection of Extirpation, which walks through our framework for inferring local extinction using a tutorial dataset from Galiano Island. The protocol is described in full in our article in Plants, People, Planet. Aspects of this protocol have been adapted in the bioReportR framework, with examples presented here for the Átl’ḵa7tsem/Howe Sound Biosphere and Saanich Peninsula.
Xetthecum: a learning journey follows the Xetthecum ecocultural mapping pilot at Retreat Cove, Galiano Island, through its three phases, from November 2020 to April 2024.

Projects tracking biodiversity change in places across the Salish Sea. Choose a place to see the projects within it.
Átl’ḵa7tsem/Howe Sound 1 Flora of Átl’ḵa7tsem/Howe Sound Explore A map-based report on the vascular plant diversity of the Átl’ḵa7tsem/Howe Sound Biosphere Region, drawing on historical collections and community science observations to relate the region’s plants to biogeoclimatic zones and protected areas, map their status, track species that have not been reported in recent decades, and recognise the contributors whose records make this work possible.
We respectfully acknowledge that this work takes place on the unceded territory of the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation), who have cared for these lands and waters since time immemorial.
Galiano Island 3 Biodiversity Galiano Island Explore A community initiative, begun in 2016, documenting the flora and fauna of Galiano Island. Hundreds of participants have recorded over 3,500 species, combining historical records with contemporary observations from iNaturalist. These baselines are being formalized in a series of biodiversity data papers with dozens of research scientists, and serve as a model for community biodiversity research across the Salish Sea.
Protocol for the Detection of Extirpation Explore Developed on Galiano Island, this protocol for detecting local extinction, or extirpation, combines historical specimens, community science observations and targeted searches. Weighing the search effort spent in each species' historical and potential habitat, the protocol tests the hypothesis that a population has been lost, in line with IUCN extinction criteria. Published in Plants, People, Planet.
Xetthecum Ecocultural Mapping Pilot Explore A pilot project, carried out by IMERSS with Indigenous and non-Indigenous collaborators through the Spirit of the Sxwo’le Coalition, to create an ecocultural map of Xetthecum (Retreat Cove), Galiano Island. Running from 2020 to 2024, the pilot wove together Indigenous ways of knowing and Western ecological science, drawing on historical and contemporary biodiversity data, terrestrial ecosystem mapping, written and spoken Hul’q’umi’num’, and stories of place—in support of a holistic approach to shle’muxun—“guardian of the land,” or “stewardship.”
Documentation: Xetthecum: a learning journey
This work was guided by the Indigenous-led Whiteswan Environmental through its Spirit of the Sxwo’le (SOS) Coalition, a cross-cultural community of practice grounded in protocols of respect and reciprocity. We are grateful for funding provided by the Indigenous Watersheds Initiative, the Inclusive Design Research Centre, the Southern Gulf Islands Community Resource Centre, and the Capital Regional District in support of this ecocultural mapping pilot.
Galiano Island is located within the shared, asserted, and unceded traditional territories of the Pune’luxutth’, Quw’utsun’, Lamalchi, W̱SÁNEĆ, Hul’q’umi’num’ and SENĆOŦEN-speaking people, and on the territories of the Coast Salish people of Galiano. The island also lies within the shared, asserted, and ceded traditional territories of the Tsawwassen First Nation. These nations, along with other Hwulmuhw Mustimuhw, continue to serve as the stewards of these lands and waters, having held rights and responsibilities here since time immemorial.
W̱SÁNEĆ/Saanich Peninsula 1 Flora of the W̱SÁNEĆ/Saanich Peninsula Explore An analysis of the vascular plant flora of the Saanich Peninsula, drawing on historical collections and community science observations to map the status of the region’s plants, track species that have not been reported in recent decades, and recognise the contributors whose records make this work possible. This work builds on the foundation of Harvey Janszen’s revisions of Szczawinski and Harrison’s (1972) Flora of the Saanich Peninsula through ongoing data curation involving a community of naturalists in the Salish Sea.
This project is undertaken in partnership with Paige Erickson-Mcgee of Habitat Acquisition Trust and Cara Gibson of Swan Lake Nature Sanctuary. We especially thank Ian Cruickshank, Matt Fairbarns, Frank Lomer, Terry Ludwar, Andy MacKinnon, Adam Martin, Emma Menchions, James Miskelly, and Kristen Miskelly for their direct contributions. We are grateful for funding provided by the Sitka Foundation, the Capital Regional District, Nature Victoria, and Keefer Ecological Services Ltd. in support of this project.
We respectfully acknowledge that this work takes place within the territories of the W̱SÁNEĆ Peoples and the Lək̓ʷəŋən (Songhees and Xʷsepsəm/Esquimalt) Peoples, who have cared for these lands and waters since time immemorial.
